# EVPI, EVPPI and EVSI: value of information for the Hanoi school garden decision

Value-of-information (VoI) analysis of a real decision model: should urban
Hanoi schools build a school garden, with or without a formal STEM education
programme, rather than keep using the land for play space or parking? The
model is the CODAS / NIFAM school garden model of @whitney2026garden
(original code: [nifam_codas_school_garden](https://github.com/CWWhitney/nifam_codas_school_garden)),
and the analysis is split front end / back end:

- Front end, [decisionSupport](https://cran.r-project.org/package=decisionSupport):
  the 84 uncertain inputs are defined in
  [inputs/school_garden_estimate.csv](inputs/school_garden_estimate.csv) as
  90%-confidence intervals with a distribution shape (`estimate_read_csv()`);
  values combine figures reported in the underlying studies with structured
  estimates from experts and estimation tools where no study exists.
  `mcSimulation()` propagates them through the model in
  [functions/school_garden_model.R](functions/school_garden_model.R) to give a Monte
  Carlo sample of inputs and payoffs (net present value, NPV, in million VND
  relative to the no-garden use of the land).
- Back end, [voi](https://chjackson.github.io/voi/): `evpi()`, `evppi()` and
  `evsi()` compute the value-of-information measures from that sample. The
  Pareto trade-offs (economic return, child health, biodiversity) are
  extracted with [rPref](https://cran.r-project.org/package=rPref).

This file is generated from [README.Rmd](README.Rmd); references come from


## What EVPI, EVPPI and EVSI mean

Choose the decision with the largest *expected* payoff, classical decision theory [@raiffa1961].

**EVPI** — how much better off we'd be, on average, if we could see every
uncertain input's true value before deciding, versus deciding now (e.g. "do
nothing").

**EVPPI** — the same idea for one input (or group), while the rest stay
uncertain; introduced to health-economic modelling by @felli1998. For example, learning one input doesn't also reveal the others, so we still need to average over the others before deciding. Inputs can also be individually worthless but jointly
decisive (see the grouped EVPPI below). `voi::evppi()` estimates this with a regression
fitted to the Monte Carlo sample [@strong2014].

**EVSI** — the value of one specific, realistic study that only partially
reduces uncertainty (e.g. a survey of schools), as opposed to perfect
information. It needs a model of how the study's data arise and update our
beliefs. `voi::evsi()` uses the regression method of @strong2015. A study
informing only one input is worth no more than perfect knowledge of that
input, which is worth no more than perfect knowledge of everything.

Net value of sampling is EVSI minus study cost: an expensive study can have
positive EVSI but negative net value. See @heath2017, @jackson2022, or the
book by @heath2024 for fuller treatments.

## The school garden decision

The decision problems are private schools and public schools, each choosing
between no garden (payoff 0 by construction), a garden, and a garden with a
formal STEM programme. Public schools additionally face the chance that they
have no land access, that the land is unsuitable, or that bureaucratic
barriers stop the project; in those cases there are no benefits.

```r
garden_mc <- decisionSupport::mcSimulation(
  estimate = decisionSupport::estimate_read_csv("inputs/school_garden_estimate.csv"),
  model_function = school_garden_function,
  numberOfModelRuns = 10000, functionSyntax = "plainNames")
private <- cbind(no_garden = 0, garden = garden_mc$y$NPV_garden_inclusive,
                 garden_STEM = garden_mc$y$NPV_garden_STEM_inclusive)
voi::evpi(private)
```

### EVPI

| School | Best option now | Expected NPV | EVPI |
|--------|-----------------|-------------:|-----:|
| Private | garden | 1417 | ~36 |
| Public | garden | 545 | ~195 |

Public schools have far more to gain from resolving uncertainty, because the
garden can fail altogether.

### EVPPI

Almost all single inputs have an EVPPI close to zero, even though the EVPI is
large. Two likely reasons (not separately tested here): the plain garden is the
best option in most of the input space, so no single input changes the
decision often; and much of the EVPI is *irreducible randomness inside each
run* (`chance_event()` and `vv()` draws: whether this school's land turns out
to be unsuitable, year-to-year variation), which no parameter study can
resolve. A clairvoyant forecast of those events is not scientific knowledge.

For the top five inputs per school type, `value_of_information.Rmd` adds bootstrap standard
errors (`evppi(se = TRUE)`) and cross-checks with the `earth` and `bart`
regression methods (`outputs/evppi_robustness.csv`), million VND:

| School | Input | `gam` | SE | `earth` | `bart` |
|--------|-------|------:|---:|--------:|-------:|
| Public | `school_event_value` | 4.2 | 2.7 | 4.9 | 3.7 |
| Public | `bureaucratic_barriers` | 1.9 | 0.9 | 2.7 | 4.1 |
| Public | `if_community_likes` | 0.9 | 1.4 | 2.4 | 0.7 |
| Private | all five inputs | < 0.1 | | < 0.1 | < 0.4 |

Only `bureaucratic_barriers` is more than two standard errors above zero.
`school_event_value` is similar in size across all three methods but its
standard error is large, and every other input is indistinguishable from
zero. The private-school EVPPIs are zero to within the noise. All of these
are tiny next to the public-school EVPI (~195), so the supported conclusion
is that no single input is worth resolving on its own, and that
`bureaucratic_barriers` is the most credible candidate. Grouped EVPPI
(`outputs/evppi_groups.csv`) for the three land-access and bureaucracy
probabilities is ~3 (`gam`) to ~5 (`earth`) for public schools. The residuals
of the `school_event_value` fit are checked with `voi::check_regression()`
(shown in `value_of_information.Rmd`).

### EVSI, population value and net benefit of sampling

An illustrative study surveys `n` public schools to learn how often
bureaucratic barriers stop a garden, using a custom binomial data generator
(`datagen_fn`) with `voi::evsi()`. Per school, EVSI rises to about 2 million
VND at n = 100, close to the EVPPI of this input (1.9 +/- 0.9), but it is
non-monotonic at small n (about 1.0 at n = 10, 0.6 at n = 20), which is
regression noise, not a real effect.

EVSI is per school; the survey pays off only if enough schools use the
result. `voi::pop_voi()` and `voi::enbs()` scale it to a population over a
time horizon. **The number of schools deciding is not taken from any source**:
`outputs/enbs_by_population.csv` shows a grid (10 to 5000 schools), and
`outputs/evsi_breakeven_schools.csv` gives the number of schools that must
face the decision for each survey to break even. With the illustrative
assumptions (5-year horizon, 5% continuous discounting, study cost 2 + 0.5
per school surveyed, million VND) a survey of 100 schools breaks even at
about 6 schools using the result. These break-even counts are small
because the per-school EVSI is of the order of 1-2 million VND, but that
EVSI is itself uncertain (standard error about 0.9 on the matching EVPPI),
so the break-even numbers should be read as an order of magnitude only.
Replace the cost, horizon, discount rate and school count with real values
before drawing conclusions.

### Pareto trade-offs

A simpler post hoc view, alongside EVPI/EVPPI/EVSI: which draws of the Monte Carlo sample are not
dominated on all three objectives at once (economic return, child health, biodiversity), using
`rPref::psel()` (`outputs/pareto_summary.csv`).

## Other things to keep in mind

- Separate learnable parameter uncertainty from irreducible randomness (e.g.
  future weather): average over the latter before computing EVPI, or a
  clairvoyant forecast of random events gets valued as scientific knowledge.
- `voi`'s regression methods are approximate: cross-check more than one
  `method` before trusting a single number for a real decision.
- If inputs are correlated, pass that structure to `estimate_read_csv()`
  (see `?estimate_read_csv`) rather than sampling independently.

## Packages

- [decisionSupport](https://cran.r-project.org/package=decisionSupport)
  (front end) [@luedeling2025decisionsupport]: also has `chance_event()`
  (risky events), `vv()` (year-to-year variation) and `discount()`
  (discounting cash flows).
- [voi](https://chjackson.github.io/voi/) (back end) [@jackson2024voi]:
  EVPPI/EVSI methods include `"gam"`, `"gp"`, `"bart"`, `"earth"`, `"inla"`
  (EVPPI) and regression, `"is"`, `"mm"` (EVSI).
- [BCEA](https://gianluca.statistica.it/software/bcea/) and
[SAVI](https://github.com/Sheffield-Accelerated-VoI/SAVI) for
cost-effectiveness-analysis-style outputs or a web interface.
